RAJYA SABHA f 12th May, 2000] 
Condition of Mahila Anganwadis 
†*661. SHRI SWARAJ KAUSHAL: Will the Minsiter of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of Mahila Anganwadis functioning in the country; 
(b) the total number of employees/offic ers working in Mahila 
Anganwadis and the details of their pay and allowances; 
(c) whether Government have received any representations regarding 
the condition of Mahila Anganwadis; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) the steps taken by Government to improve their condition? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT, 
MINISTER OF SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY AND MINISTER OF 
OCEAN DEVELOPMENT (DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) to (e) A 
Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) A total of 513072 Anganwadi Centr es are presently functioning in  
the country. 
(b) Each Anganwadi Centre is managed by an Anganwadi Worker 
assisted by an Anganwadi Helper. These Workers are part -time honorary 
workers who get monthly honorarium ranging from Rs. 438 to Rs. 563 
depending upon the  length of engagement and qualification for Anganwadi 
Workers and Rs. 260 for Anganwadi Helpers. The details are provided in the 
Table-I (See below). Some State Governrnent/UT Administrations are also 
providing additional honorarium to these the Workers from their own resources. 
The details are provided in Table- II (See below). There are no employees/ 
officers working in the Anganwadis. 
(c) and (d) The Government has been receiving representations from 
various organisations] individuals, Anganwadi Worker Associations and Union 
etc. The representations are mainly for the increase in the amount of the 
honorarium being paid to them, declaring them as Government Servants 
recruitment of Anganwadi Workers as Supervisor, additional remuneration 
for additional work, non- transfer of the Scheme to Private Agencies or 
Panchayats. 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
4 

[ 12th May, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
(e) The Government has been constantly endeavouring for the betterment 
of the working conditions of Anganwadi Workers and Helpers. Honorarium 
of Anganwadi Workers and Helpers has been enhanced from time to time. 
The honorarium was enhanced during 1978, 1986 and 1992. In May, 1997 
the honorarium of Anganwadi Workers and Helpers was further enhanced by 
25% and 30%  respectively and the honorarium ranges from Rs. 438/ - to Rs. 
563/- per month depending on the qualification and length of engagement for 
Anganwadi Workers and Rs. 260/ - per month for Anganwadi Helpers. Apart 
from the honorarium, the Anganwadi Workers & Helpers are also getting two 
time paid absence of 3 month each on maternity, one time paid absence of 42 
days in case of abortion/miscarriage, 20 days paid casual absence per year, 
travelling reimbursement/D.A. for attending meetings etc. State Governments/ 
UT Administrations have also been requested to reserve at least 25% posts of 
Supervisors to be recruited from eligible Anganwadi Workers. In 1999, the 
board and lodging norms for attending training programmes have been revised. 
They have also been allowed to avail.one month additional honorarium for 
completing the pre-service training.

Expenditure on Eradication on Malaria 
*662. SHRI DRUPAD BORGOHAIN: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) what policy the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has adopted 
to eradicate Malaria from the country, whether there is any specific plan for 
North-Eastern Region's malaria prone zone; and 
11 

RAJYA SABHA [ 12th May, 2000] 
(b) what amount has been spent for eradicating Malaria from the country 
in different States and UTs during the last three years? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (S HRI N.T. SHANMUGAM): (a) and (b) A statement 
is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) For control of malaria, a national programme, namely, National 
Anti-Malaria Programme (NAMP) is being implemented in the country 
generally as a Category -II Centrally sponsored Scheme on cost -sharing basis 
between the Centre and the States. However, for the North -eastern States this 
programme is 100% Centrally finance since December, 1994. 
The specific strategy adopted for control of Malaria under the NAMP 
includes:—  
* Intensification of vector control measures through prioritization of areas 
for selective spray with appropriate insecticides and alternative and 
integrated vector control methods in rural areas. 
* Intensification of anti larval operation in urban areas. 
* Early detection and prompt treatment of cases. 
* Intensification of Information, Education & Communication (IEC) 
activities for creating public awareness and mobilizing community 
participation. 
* Manpower development through intensive training and re -orientation 
programmes at all levels and efficient Management Information System 
(MIS). 
In addition, an Enhanced Malaria Control Project (EMCP) with World  
Bank support, essentially covering 1045 PHCs in 100 pre -dominantly tribal  
districts which are malaria endemic in  the States of Andhra Pradesh, Bihar,  
Gujarat, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradsh, Orissa and Rajasthan and 19 Cities/  
Towns in these States and also falling in the States of Karnataka, Tamil Nadu  
and West Bengal is being implemented since September, 1997. This pr oject 
aims at intensifying malaria control activities by way of additional inputs  
through a mix of interventions such as:  
* Early case Detection and Prompt Treatment (EDPT) through use of  
newer drugs like Artemesenin and Rapid Diagnostic kits. 
12 

[ 12th May, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
* Selective Vector Control including use of Synthetic Pyrethroids in rural 
areas and Biolarvicides in urban areas. 
* Promotion of persona! protection methods by use of Medicated Mosquito 
Nets (MMNs)  
* Early detection and containment of epidemics. 
* Information, Education and Communication towards personal 
prevention and Community participation. 
Institutional and Management capacity building, manpower 
development through intensive re -orientation training" programmes at 
all levels and efficient Management Information System (MIS) 
* Annual Programme Development Review (APDR) is an integral part of 
the EMCP. 
The components of Human Resource Development (HRD), Management 
Information System (MIS) and Information Education Communication (IEC) 
are common for the whole country. The project also has a flexibility to divert 
resources from the core project areas (100 districts) to any part of the country 
in case of outbreaks and/or epidemics. 
(b) Requisite information is given at Statement-I.

SHRI DRUPAD BORG OHAIN: Sir, in the performance hudget lor 
2000-2001 of the Ministry of Health, it is stated that about 2 million cases of 
malaria are recorded annually since 1984. But it is much more in reality, as

people belong to below the poverty line. These people do not report at the 
health centres. So, to prevent malaria parasites from being transmitted by the 
mosquitoes, spraying of DDT, Malathion and synthetic pyrethroid is being 
done. But the success on the part of the Government is only 60%. It is reported

pyrethroids. But the implementing agency is the State Governments, who 
sometimes release the budgeted amount a little later. There is also a shortage of

fully utilise  the budget amount; and sometimes some States spend the

Preparation of New Curriculum by NCERT 
*668. SHRI EDUARDO FALEIRO: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) Whether NCERT has been asked to prepare a new national curriculum 
framework for schools; 
(b) if so, the directions that have been given to NCERT in preparing the 
new curriculum framework; and 
(c) whether the new curriculum would be placed before the Central  
Advisory Board of Education (CABE) for apaproval, before it is finalised?  
THE; MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (DR. MURLI 
MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) to (c) A statement is laid on the Table of the Sabha. 
Statement 
(a) The National Policy on Education —1986 [as updated in 1992] and 
Programme of Action— 1992 stipulate that there should be curriculum renewal 
before the end of the 8th Five year Plan period. In pursuance of the same and 
similar recommendations of the Ninth Plan document in this regard, NCERT 
[an autonomous organisation of Department of Education] has prepared a 
"Discussion Document' on National Curriculum Frame work for School 
Education. Previously, NCERT had brought out the ""National Curriculum 
for Elementary and Secondary Education, A Framework' in 1988. 
(b) No directions have been given to NCERT for preparing the discussion 
Document. 
(c) After due deliberations across the country, as soon as NCERT finalises 
the document, it shall be palced before the Central Government for approval, 
after a formal consultation with the State Governments. 
SHRI EDUARDO FALEIRO: I would like to know why the new 
curriculum has not been pl aced before the Central Advisory Board of 
Education, that is, CABC. I think this is really a forum where a discussion can 
take place, rather than dealing with it on one -to-one basis with the States. 
When we are having a conference of all the State Educatio n Ministers here, I 
think it is the best way fo dealing with an issue which is of national educational 
significance. It is a crucial issue and is of national educational significance. 
DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI: The NCERT has prepared a document 
of discussion and they are discussing it with various broads and agencies. 
24 

112th May, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
When they finalise the document and come before the Government, we will 
certainly take it into consideration. 
SHRI EDUARDO FALEIRO: Sir, part (b) of my question is this. At 
what stage is the discussion on? Will the hon -Minister also place this very 
important document before Parliament for a discussion? 
DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI: This document is rearding the 
updating of curriculum, and, to the best of my knowledge, updating of 
curriculum has never been placed before Parliament. But if the hon. Member 
wants to discuss it, I would be very happy to discuss it in the House, but I 
think it has never been done before. Under the Education Policy, it is mandatory 
for the NCE RT to update the curricula after every five years. This is their 
mandatory work which they are doing.

*674. SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHARJEE: Wil l the Minister of 
HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
40 

[ 12th May, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news -item, 
captioned "India accounts for 40 p.c. malnourished kids", published in the 
'Hindu' dated 21st April, 2000; 
(b) if so, whether the reasons for this poor rate of child nutrition have 
been identified; and 
(c) what steps are proposed to be taken in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT, 
MINISTER OF SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY AND MINISTER OF 
OCEAN DEVELOPMENT (DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) The nutritional status of children is an outcome of complex 
and inter-related set of factors. 
It follows a cycle, which begins with low birth weight of an infant caused 
by the malnourishme nt of the mother. Thereafter, delayed and inadequate 
complementary feeding of the malnourished infant results in further aggravation 
of malnutrition. Poor child caring practices because of female illiteracy and 
ignorance about nutrition and health worsen t he situation. Further, gender 
discrimination against the girl child in terms of nutrition and healthcare leads 
of a malnourished adolescent girl who is married early. When the girl is still a 
child, she has to bear the burden of motherhood resulting in bir th of 
malnourished infants. This perpetuates an inter -generational cycle of 
malnutrition. 
The socio -economic factors which adversely affect the nutritional 
situation of children are illiteracy, particularly of women, food insecurity at 
household level, poor status of women, poor access to health care, safe'drinking 
water and sanitation, and high rate of population growth. 
These reasons of child malnutrition are well established through several 
studies. 
As stated above, the problem of malnutrition is a multi-sectoral one and 
is being addressed by the concerned departments/ministries of the Government. 
The Department of Women and Child Development runs the ICDS 
scheme which covers around 75% of the development blocks and urban slums 
in the country at present. Under this scheme, a nutrition supplement is provided 
to children up to the age of six years who attend the Anganwadi Centres, 
41

pregnant women and lactating women, and in some development blocks, 
adolescent girls. The nutrition supplement under the scheme is provided by 
the State Governments and in some areas by the CARE and WFR 
Under the mandate of the National Nutrition Policy, it is proposed to 
have a National Nutrition Mission for addressing the whole issue of malnutrition 
in a more comprehensive, inter-generational manner.

5042. DR. ALLADI P. RAJKUMAR: Will the Minister of CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state the action  
proposed to ensure that people below poverty line actually get the benefit of  
PDS and not t he middlemen/traders, who are the beneficiaries as ration items  
reach the market place? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHRIRAM CHAUHAN): 
Public Distribution System is implemented under the joint resp onsibility of 
the Central and State Governments/UT Administrations. The Central 
Government is respons'ible for procurement, storage and transportation of the 
PDS commodities up to the central godowns and making them available to the 
States. The responsibility for distribution to the consumers through the Fair 
Price Shops and administration of PDS rests with the State Governments and 
UT Administrations. A series of measures have been taken by Government of 
India to ensure that people living below poverty line actually get the benefit of 
PDS. 
State Governments have been requested to closely monitor PDS at the 
Fair Price Shop (FPS) and other levels to curb diversion and to make 
arrangement for distribution of PDS commodities in a transparent and 
accountable man ner by involving Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) in 
implementation of PDS. They have been asked to eliminate bogus ration cards 
and bogus units in the ration cards. The State Governments have also been 
advised to initiate action against erring FPS owner s under Essential 
Commodities Act, 1955. A model Citizens' Charter for PDS has also been 
drawn up and circulated to States/UTs for adoption in order that there is 
transparency and accountability in the system so that PDS commodities reach 
the targeted bene ficiaries efficiently. The Government of India has also 
appointed Area Officers to States/UTs to monitor the functioning of PDS 
including complaints of diversion.

Reduction in driage allowance of par-boiled rice 
J046.    SARDAR GURCHARAN SINGH TOHRA: 
SHRI SUKHDEV SINGH LIBRA: 
Will the Minister  of CONSUMER AFFAIRS AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have totally disallowed driag e allowance, 
permissible earlier, on par-boiled rice; 
(b) whether Government have also reduced driage allowance from two 
per cent to one per cent for manufacture of raw rice; and 
(c) if so, the scientific reasons for taking such a decision? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHRIRAM 
CHAUHAN): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Yes, Sir. 
(c) The expert Committee on rice milling  (Gokak Committee)  
appointed by Government of India, had not recommended any driage  
allowances for both r aw an par -boiled rice as it had taken this factor into  
consideration while fixing the out -turn ratio of raw and par -boiled rice.  
The Committee observed that during par -boiling operations, irrespective of  
moisture content the paddy imbibes, water and the ov erall moisture content  
will increase to an extent of 28 to 35 percent. During drying operations, the  
same is reduced to milliable level of moisture content and the same is  
between 12 to 15 percent. In view of such change, there is no justillable  
reason for  allowing any driage loss due to reduction in moisture content  
during storage for milling par -boiled paddy. However, considering that some  
driage in paddy takes place before the same is milled, a driage of two percent  
in raw rice was allowed in case of Pun jab in 1998- 99. The same has been  
reduced to one percent for all the States for Custom Milling of Paddy for  
production of raw rice as decided by the Government on 1st December,  
1998.

Seminar on combined waste water Treatment 
5069. SHRI YADLAPATl VENKAT RAO: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Ministry sponsored an international seminar on combined 
waste water treatment at Hyderabad during March, 2000. 
(b) if so, the salient features of the views expressed on waste water 
management and regulatory aspects; and 
(c) the measures proposed to implement the views'? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS (SHRI BABU LAL MARANDI): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The salient features of the views expressed on waste water  
management and regulatory aspects are outlined below:—  
— There should be concerted efforts to set up combined waste water 
treatment plants instead of the common effluent treatment plants as 
the addition of sewage to the industrial waste water improves overall 
treatability. 
— All efforts should be made to construct/strengthen the terminal waste 
water treatemnt facility to meet the required disposal standards. The 
sharing of capital cost and the cost of treatment at such facilities could 
be on equitable basis between the municipality and industry. 
— All efforts should be made to recycle and reuse the, treated waste waters 
at the industry/terminal treatment stage. 
— In plant controls  and cleaner technologies of production leading to 
waste minimisation should be encouraged through incentives/ 
disincentives. 
— Concentration of total dissolved solids in waste water is a serious 
problem and requires to be addressed in depth. 
— The regulatory agencies should initiate investigative studies to assess 
the effect of the treated effluent on the receiving environment. 
(c) The aim of the seminar was to facilitate exchange of views and  
experience and create better awareness in regard to combined waste water 
treatment among the participants which would ultimately help in implementation.

FOG Due to Air Pollution 
5073. SHRI PARMESHWAR KUMAR AGARWALLA: Will the Minister 
of ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that increased amount of fog in winter is mainly 
due to increase in air pollution; 
(b) if so, what is the pollution level detected in the air during the recent 
winter; 
(c) whether trend shows deteriorating situation year after year; and 
(d) what comprehensive plans are proposed to be taken to arrest this trend? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS (SHRI BABU LAL MARANDI): (a) and (b) Atmospheric 
pollutants act as a source of condensation nuclei and help in the formation of 
fog. However, there is no one to one correspondence between formation of fog 
and air pollution because the meteorological conditions required for formation 
of fog may not always be satisfied. Fog may be dense over unpolluted rural 
surroundings due to radiation cooling of the earth's surface. 
(c)The occurrence of fog over North-West India during winter, particularly 
December and January, is a common phenomenon. No definite trend, either 
increasing decreasing, in the occurrence of fog has been observed during the 
last 10 years. 
(d) Does not arise.

5135. SHRI R.S.GAVAI: 
SHRI RAMDAS AGARWAL: 
SHRI PARMESHWAR KUMAR AGARWALLA:

(a) whether Government have achieved a break-through in sea bed mining 
technology; 
162 

[ 12th May, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) by when commercial mining would start with this technology and 
what would be its financial viability; 
 
(d) the details of the m etals explored under polymetallic nodules 
programmes so far, item-wise; and 
(e) the expenditure incurred on this programme? 
THE MINISTER OF OCEAN DEVELOPMENT (DR. MURLI 
MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) to (c) Under a joint technology demonstration 
programme for development  of Deep Sea Mining System with Institute for 
Konstruction (IKS), University of Siegen, Germany, the Department of Ocean 
Development through its autonomous institution namely National Institute of 
Ocean Technology, has designed a crawler mounted mining system with special 
rubber tracks, umbilical cable with an outer steel armour which carries the 
weight of the vehicle during launch and retrieval and transmits power and 
signals to the system during operation, a number of transducers for monitoring 
the speed,  direction, stability, pump performance etc., special under water 
cameras to observe the mining area, etc. The design of the crawler also involves 
complex integration of mechanical, electrical and instrumentation technologies 
and is a break through providi ng a firm basis for the development of a Deep 
Sea Mining System. While the system in its final form will be capable of 
operating up to 6,000 m water depth, in the initial stages the system has been 
successfully demonstrated at a depth of 410 m off Tuticori n in the east coast 
during March, 2000. It is likely to take about 5 years from now on to establish 
its technical capabilities, commercial and economic viability. 
(d) An area of 150,000 sq. km. allotted by the International Sea Bed 
Authority of the United Nati ons in the Central Indian Ocean Basin (CIOB) to 
India as a Pioneer Investor in polymetallic nodules programme has been 
surveyed. As per estimates made though this exploratory survey there is a 
potential of about 380 million tones of nodules in CIOB mine site allotted to 
India, comprising about 3 million tones of copper, 3.2 million tones of nickel, 
0.49 million tones of cobalt and 73 million tones of manganese, which could 
be exploited by developing suitable sophisticated deep sea mining technologies. 
(e) For this shallow bed mining technology development programme a 
sum of about Rs. 15.00 crore has been spent so far, during the 9th Plan 
period.

Railway Transport Planning 
5159. SHRI BRATIN SENGUPTA: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) Whether it is a fact that Indian Railways do not have any machinery to 
collect data on the performance of its competitors, the Roadways; 
(b) Whether it is also a fact that in this age of information technology, 
Indian Railways have no informa tion on movement of non -bulk materials 
through Roadways; and 
(c) Whether the Railway transport planning is done in darkness and without 
any care for the economic interest of this nation. 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) to (c) While Railway maintain comprehensive 
records of the traffic carried by them, Roadways are not similarly organised to 
maintain these data. Some estimates prepared by committee / experts groups, 
based on certain assumptions are, however, available. The latest estimates from 
the Planning Commission are available only for 1995. According to these 
estimates the share of railways in the land freight traffic is about 40%. 
Railway Transport Planning is based on total requirement of traffic and 
available resources for capacity augmentation. In order to increase the Railway's 
share in the total transportation, Railways have planned for a market-driven 
180 

[12th May, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
and customer -focussed approach. To achieve this, Railways' policy 
contemplates strengthening the Railways' presence in the long -haul bulk 
movement and containerised cargo segments. With a view to recapturing the 
piece-meal, high rated general cargo, CONCOR's domestic division has started 
new service named "CONTRACK" in 1997. In  the railway budget for 2000-
01, the railways have set an objective to raise the rail share of freight traffic 
from 40% to 50% during the first decade of the new millennium. Achievement 
of this target will require a substantian augmentation of the line and  terminal 
capacity on the saturated "High -Density Network", and a multi- pronged new 
Freight Policy with the following elements: 
* Recovering non-bulk high value traffic through appropriate marketing 
effors. 
* Providing incentives like "volume discount scheme". 
* Offering the leasing route to Freight Forwarders in the Luggage Vans 
(SLRs) on popular mail and express trains. 
* Facilitating warehousing at existing railway terminals as a marketing 
tool to attract traffic. 
* Extending the new concept of Roll -On-Roll-Off (R O-RO) in freight 
movement. Trucks rolled on to flat wagons will be transported by Rail 
and unloaded from wagons at destinations to provide door to door 
collection and delivery. This has been successfully launched on the 
Konkan Railway. 
* Running of fixed schedule freight trains and terminal operations. 
* Launching the "Freight Operations Information System" (FOIS) to 
provide real -time information to customers in regard to booking, 
movement and delivery of freight consignments through Customer 
Service Cells to be set up on all Zonal Railways. 
* Using the shadow-path created behind fast moving mail / express trains 
for speedy movement of freight traffic. High speed goods trains are 
slated to follow Superfast express trains with adequate safety precautions 
to ensure expeditious transit of select high value and perishable goods.

(i) To help India become an inventive and creative society Jind a global

sustaining and scaling up grassroot green innovations and helping their 
transition to self supporting activities, seeking self reliance through competitive 
advantage of innovation based enterprises and/or application of people 
generated sustainable technologies at grassroot level. 
(iv) To evolve strategies and conduct, co -ordinate and support research, 
design and development efforts in the country on grassroot innovations so as 
to attain and maintain technological competence and enhance self reliance. 
To build linkages between excellence in formal scientific systems and informal 
knowledge systems and create a Knowledge Network to link various 
stakeholders through application of information technologies and also 
otherwise.

non-commercial applications of know -how generated as a result of 1 to 4.

sharing, of innovators, and encourage their incorporation in educational

Sir, the main reasons for decline in the level of ground water are: 
(i) Rapid pace of urbanisation has resulted in reduction in 
recharge of aquifers.    Pervious areas have become less 
pervious. 
(ii) Increasing demand in agricultural and industrial sectors as 
well as domestic needs for the ever growing population 
results in high stress on ground water. 
(iii) Change in cropping pattern in order to raise water intensive crops 
has resulted in over -exploitation of ground water in certain 
areas.

embankments, water storage and water power, being a State subject, action 
to augment ground water resources is to be taken by the State Governments. 
However, the steps taken by the Union Government to increase the ground 
water level in the country include: 
(i) The Central Ground Water Authority has been constituted 
under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 for regulation 
and control of ground water management and development 
throughout the country. 
(ii) The Central Ground Water Board has undertaken a Central 
sector scheme on pilot basis on artificial recharge of ground

scheme is not made. Funds are provided to States for 
construction of civil works for recharge structures on cost -

The Government have formulated a centrally -sponsored 
scheme to assist the States in Artificial Recharge of ground 
water at an estimated cost of Rs. 101.50 crores. This 
Scheme is at consultation stage in t he Planning 
Commission. 
A model Bill has been circulated to all the States/Union Territories, to 
enable them to enact suitable legislation for regulation and control of ground 
water development. 
A manual on Artificial Recharge of ground water has been circ ulated to 
the States/Union Territories to enable them to formulate area specific Artificial 
Recharge Schemes to check the declining trend in ground water levels. 
A national perspective plan for recharge of ground water by utilising 
surplus monsoon runoff has been prepared. 
With a view to promoting the roof top rain water harvesting, the Ministry 
of Water Resources has proposed to the Ministry of Urban Development to 
consider making suitable regulations for roof top rain water harvesting for

years of Independence and India being one of the fastest growing countries in 
the world, it is a matter of grave concern for us that we have not been able to 
even assure hygienic water supply to half of the population. Our existing water

Government after Government have assured this nation, time and again, about 
ensuring supply of hygienic water to all the vil lages in the country, but it is still 
a dream. I am not involving politics in this. But, it is a matter of fact and 
thereby, it is a matter of serious concern for all of us. It may be interesting to 
note that if only 10 per cent of our water resources are properly utilized, 100 
per cent of our population can have assured supply of water which is hygienic 
and good in every respect. But, unfortunately, nothing has been done in this 
direction. Now that we have crossed the one-billion population mark, the time

responsibility of managing water resources to the States and Union Territories 
and the States and the Union Territories have, in turn, prepared schemes on 
paper and sent to the Central Government for assistance. What has been 
going on for the last 50 years is like a foot -ball game, the Central Government 
holding the States responsible and the States holding the Central Government 
responsible.

20 years, in some of the districts in our country, the water table has gone

cropping pattern to water -intensive crops are the reasons which are stated 
here. They are absolutely correct. I don't want to deny them. This alarming 
situation has been the product of indiscriminate exploitation of the ground 
water. It is like a bank account. If you withdraw the amount continuously, the 
balance will dwindle. The same is the case with water resources also. It is a 
very scarce resource. The Government has treated it absolutely as a private 
source. The farmers or the consumers are allowed to exploit the water 
resources indiscriminately without any control by the Government. All the 
successive Governments did not have any vision. Had they got any vision and 
regulated it, the present state of affairs would not have arisen. This has got 
very dangerous social consequences. I will give you one example. The rural 
rich fanners are exploiting the situation. The poor farmers are unable to sink 
bbrewells and exploit.the water for one acre or two acres of land. The very 
well-to-do households in urban areas are only capable of exploiting the 
groundwater. A survey says 37 per cent of the rural population and 32 per cent 
of the urban population are below the poverty line. They are absolutely unable 
to exploit the ground water. As the poor farmers are unable to exploit the 
groundwater, they have to depend on the water supplied by the big farmers 
who got the water resources. Since the poor farmers are not in a position to 
get the water, they are giving on lease or selling their lands to the big farmers 
and they themsleves become the agricultural labourers. These are the social 
consequences of the situation which has been created. 
Recently, the Supreme Court has given directions to one research 
organisation, namely, the National Environmental Research Institute, to submit 
a report. In its report it is stated that in nine major Sta tes, including the bread 
baskets and rice granaries like Punjab, Haryana, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil 
Nadu, in the country widespread water depletion is going on. The annual 
depletion of water in India is 1,000 billion cubic metres. One cubic metre of 
water weighs one tonne. That is what the survey has indicated. One thousand 
tonnes of water is equal to the production of one tonne foodgrains. Unless we 
arrest this trend, we will be deprived of 180 million tonnes of foodgrains per 
annum. That is the report whic h it has submitted. I am just explaining the 
alarming nature of the situation. Even in Punjab and Haryana more than half a 
metre of water depletion is taking place every year. In the process, in the 
coastal areas, it is attracting sea-water.    Ultimately, instead of groundwater

SHRI SWARAJ KAUSHAL : Mr. Chairman, Sir, the decline in water 
level is a post-1962 phenomenon. During the years 1971-1983 - in 12 long years'- 
the water level in Delhi declined between four meters to eight meters. But, it took 
just two years ie., between 1983 and 1985, the water level declined by four 
meters to eight meters. 
Sir, we depend very heavily on monsoons and, somehow, we have 
accepted that drought and floods are in-built in to our monsoonal ecology. The- 
reason is little different. The reason for this decline in water level is that we have 
abandoned our ancient system of water management. During ancient times, as Mr. 
Kaushik has pointed out, the cities were established by the sides of the river banks; 
and other cities and towns, like Jaipur, Jodhpur, Bhopal, Jaisalmer and so on, 
collected the rain water and conserved it for use for the purpose of drinking and 
agriculture. < Mr. Minister, your statement is silent on one count and that is 
related to the contamination of the underground water. As Shri Sanjay Nirupam has 
point out, the Nitrates present in the underground water are carcinogenic in nature. 
You, being a doctor, can appreciate this that the fluorides present in the 
underground water cause neur ological problems, and the mercury present in 
the underground water is as much as 58 times than the normal standardised 
water, and this contamination is a major source of infant mortality amongst children.   
There is another problem.  The contaminated underground water 
235 

RAJYA SABHA [12 MAY, 2000]. 
cannot be cleaned because the cost is enormous.   The reason is that our 
industry considers borewells as dustbins of effluents. 
Mr. Minister, you have mentioned about water storage laws being 
incorporated into the urban development laws. Sir, Himachal Pradesh has 
already done this. I think we should examine the Himachal experience and 
have it incorporated in the urban development laws of other States. You have 
also mentioned about the creation of the Ground Wat er Authority. I am sorry, 
this was not done by the Union Government. It was done pursuant to the 
directions issued by the Supreme Court of India. In addition, the Supreme 
Court mandated in paragraph 12 of its judgement given in the case of Shri 
M.C. Mehta in 1977. We would like to know from you as to what action you 
have taken on the mandate given by the Supreme Court. That mandate says, 
"The main object of the constitution of a board, as an authority, is the urgent 
need for regulating the indiscriminate boring and withdrawal of underground 
water in the country. We have no doubt that the authority, so constituted, shall 
apply its mind to this urgent aspect of the matter and shall issue necessary 
regulatory directions." So, you are empowered to issue directions to the State 
Governments. Your role is not merely that of giving advice or consultative in 
nature. With a view to preserving and protecting the underground water, this 
aspect may be taken up by the Authority on a very, very urgent basis. That is 
the man date of the Supreme Court. You have also mentioned about the 
circulation of a model HIL It is pending for the last 30 years. When you 
circulated it first, it was in the year 1970! May I know from the hon. Minister as 
to what is the development in this regard? Shall we be mere helpless 
spectators waiting for the State Governments to act, or, shall we realise the 
need of the hour and call upon the State Governments to act quickly because 
this is the mandate of the people, this is the mandate of the country and this is 
the mandate of the Supreme Court? I again request you, Mr. Minister, that this 
British system of water management will not help. We have to resort to our 
ancient system of water management, and that survived for thousands of 
years. I think that a lone is the ultimate solution to the water problem in the 
country. Thank you, Sir. 
SHRI N. R. DASARI (Andhra Pradesh); Mr. Chairman, Sir, this Calling 
Attention motion on depleting water resources has come for discussion in this 
august House at a very righ t time when the drinking water problem has 
become very grave in India and some States have been hit by 
236 

[12 MAY, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
sever drought. 
I would like to associate myself with the ideas of my hon. colleagues on 
this problem. We have come to a s tage when tens of crores of masses are 
starving for want of drinking water. The problem of depleting water resources 
is inextricably linked with river water projects, small, medium or major. This 
will help us to raise the ground water level in some areas a s well as control 
the flooding of the rivers. The water management programme, campaigned by 
Anna Hazare in Maharashtra, has to be popularised and extended to other 
parts of the country. 
There is a large scope for exploitation of the ground water. Though a 
large portion of the available ground water resources remains untapped, over-
exploitation of the resources in some areas has created problems. After the 
hydro-geological surveys carried out during 1976-86 in twelve major States, 
namely, Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Gujarat, Haryana, Karnataka, Madhya 
Pradesh, Maharashtra, Punjab, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh and 
West Bengal, covering 627 Ijlocks, 351 blocks have been declared as dark 
blocks with over -exploitation and reduced ground water, whereas 276 bloc ks 
have been identified as grey blocks where similar problems were developing. 
Indiscriminate exploitation of ground water from such areas needs to be 
regulated through legal provisions. 
This is no longer just a rural problem. Cities too are now buckling under 
the strain of water shortage. We ought to learn from the example of rich 
industrialised countries which have incorporated conservation both in policy 
and in the daily lives of the people. Since most of the area in cities is occupied 
by buildings, conc rete floors, roads and foothpaths, the entire rain water is 
channelised into drainages. Therefore, there is an urgent need to conserve 
most of the rain water during monsoons for further use during lean periods. 
I would like to cite an example, what I have learnt from the media. In 
Madhya Pradesh, a water-shed management project based on tapping of rain 
water, has turned Jhabua into one of the greenest districts of the State. In 
another town in Madhya Pradesh, named, "Dewas," one can find a number of 
water-harvesting structures on building roofs, all raised during a one-year 
drive by an efficient District Collector. This scheme should be popularised all 
over the country. NGOs will have to play a more active role for spreading the 
message of rain-water harvesting across the country.

the Lok Sabha on the 3rd of May, 2000, has said that the proposal for 
formulation of a Central scheme to assist States in art ificial recharge of 
ground water, is still at the consultation stage. This is unfortunate.  This 
should be attended to as a priority task. 
India's ground water is being polluted by numerous factories that directly 
pump untreated effluents into the ground t hrough dry borewells. Pollution of 
ground water is as bad a crime as any other that can be perpetrated on 
human-kind. Once polluted, ground water is almost impossible to be cleaned, 
and the cost is prohibitive. The Governments, both at the Centre and in the 
States, should take effective measures to avert this increasing damages of 
pollution. Thank you.

SHRI S. AGNIRAJ (Tamil Nadu) : Mr. Vice -Chairman, Sir, for the past

per cent of the total water available for use in India is from surface runoff,

augment the water and

DR. C.P. THAKUR: Sir, at the very outset, I thank all the Members for 
taking part in the discussion, and I find that the suggestions given by the 
Members are very valuable. There is no discrepancy between the intention of 
the Government, action of the Government, the planning of the Government 
and the suggestions given by the Members. Now, Sir, the vital importance of 
water for life and civilization cannot be overs aid. The existence of water 
storage structures and water delivery system have been confirmed in earlier 
civilisations in our sub continent, such as the remains of the Harappan 
civilization. Some of the Members have referred to it in their speeches. Our 
sacred books, such as the Rigveda, recognised the importance of water in 
the cycle of life. This is also reflected in the canto of the Mahabharata which 
states that life is sustained by food, but food itself result from rain. 
The importance of water production and its structures, such as 
wells, tanks and lakes, finds mention in many books, such as the Vishnu 
Puran, the Vishwakarma Vastu Shastra and so on. The concept of water as a 
resource, which has to be managed property in the interest of public, finds a 
clear mention in the Kautilya Arthashastra which lays down the duties of the 
responsible Government in erection of water works and the regulation of water 
rights. 
With the rise in population and a significant increase in the living 
standards, its importance has become far more critical today. More 
importantly, the expectation of the people has gone up. Therefore, it is the 
duty and the responsibility of the Centre and the State Governments to 
ensure adequate availability of water, firstly, for drinking purpos es; and, then, 
for agriculture, industry and other uses.   The present water crisis in

SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO (Andhra Pradesh): In our society, unemployment 
is a matter of great worry. It has been the concern of not only the youth and the 
students who are job-seekers, but of the Government also. Unemployment causes 
frustration among the youth. We all know what a frustrated person can do. An 
unemployed person, who is frustrated, is a potential threat to the harmony and order 
of the society. We don't have to be surprised to see that due to increase in 
unemployment, the incidents of crime and terrorism have also increased.   Sir, the 
high level of population 
260 

[12 MAY, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
growth  has   resulted  in   an  unprecedented   growth   in  the  employable 
population. 
Between 1994 and 1997 the population grew at the rate of 1.89 per cent 
per annum and it reached 950 million in 1997. Today, our population is one 
billion. I don't know whether we should feel proud of having one billion 
population, or, whether we should feel ashamed. All our family planning 
programmes have gone haywire. During this period the employable 
population grew at the rate of 2.43 per cent per year and it reached the level 
of 397 million in 1997. 
According to the Ninth Five Year Plan document, there are three 
reasons which are responsible for unemployment. The extremely high rate of 
population growth in the past 15-20 years is considered as the first reason. 
The second reason is the large addition of female workers to the total labour 
force. The third reason is overall decrease in mortality rates, particularly, in 
infant mortality. 
If we look at the nature and the kind of employment that is available, we 
will find more disturbing trends. Except for a very thin layer of white-collared, 
well-paid jobs, a majority of the new entrants into the employment market are 
placed on a precarious purch. There has also been an alarming rise in the 
proportion of the people employed in the informal sector. However, the 
growth in the informal sector is not a positive indication of a growing 
economy. We cannot consider it as a regular and positive employment, 
according to international standards. 
According to ILO's World Employment Report, the employment in the 
modern manufacturing sector in India has barely increased between 1975-
1992. Though there was a faster growth of output in India, the manufacturing 
output was growing without creating regular well-paid jobs. 
In all our Five Year Plans serious concern has been expressed over the 
prevailing massive unemployment. I agree that the Planning Commission has 
always aimed at generating more employment. In spite of the several 
measures, all the promises have not been converted into actions. According 
to the decennial census data of 1981, the percentage of employed persons 
was only 36.7 per cent of our total population. This percentage of employed 
persons has increased just marginally to 37.5 per cent in 1991. 
261 

RAJYA SABHA [12 MAY, 2000] 
One of the long-term strategies that should be adopted for generating 
productive employment is to increase the skills and capabilities of the working 
population through investment in human capital . In the education front, we 
have to bring more reforms by introducing more vocational courses. I agree 
that the achievement of the target of full employment, in the present 
circumstances, seems to be very grim. But there should be, at least, a rate of 
3 per cent growth in employment so that the condition may improve. This 
would also make the target a bit realistic. For this, we should make a suitable 
mix of capital -intensive and labour -intensive technologies in various sectors. 
In addition to this, as I have already said, there should be more vocational 
and practical training in the educational institutions. This would also lead to an 
increase in the productivity of the workforce. Having said all this, it is needless 
to say now that efforts should be intens ified to reduce the rate of population 
growth. 
The present society is a computer society and the future belongs to the 
computers. There is a tremendous potential in the computer industry which is 
also known as information technology. The Government should take all 
necessary steps to bring computer training to the taluka level and the block 
level and, maybe, to the mandal level. 
If our youth are provided computer training, it will go a long way in 
creating employment opportunities and making them eligible to get 
employment in the information technology industry. Thank you very much, Sir. 
SHRI RANGANATH MISRA (Orissa): I rise to support the Bill and 
congratulate Mr. Pachouri for having brought forward this Bill. In 1947, when 
we became independent, the total p opulation of the country was about 35 
crores. We have multiplied by more than three times, almost four times, during 
these 52 years. Population and unemployment are interconnected. The 
present situation of unemployment is directly the outcome of the abnorm al 
growth in population. I am of the view that the direction, which we followed, 
after we became independent, had been on the wrong track. Priorities were 
not properly fixed. If that had been done, I am sure, we would not have landed 
ourselves in the present situation. Today, we find ourselves almost in a losing 
situation. The Constitution-makers had divided the entitlements of the citizens 
into two categories. One, the Fundamental Rights, which were put in Part III of 
the Constitution.  These are provisions 
262 

[12 MAY, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
for certain benefits and advantages which are avalable to the people, and are 
justiciable in a court of law. They put certain things in Part IV which they 
labelled as the Directive Principles of State Policy. The Fundament al Rights 
are enforceable as such. But the State Policy matters are something where 
legislation is required; then a law is made. So, they are enforceable through 
legislation. The provisions contained in Part -I V are not enforceable by court. 
Today, the matter which has been raised by Mr. Pachouri, is covered by Part -
IV, i.e. the Directive Principles of State Policy, and requires legislation. 
Discussions on this had been going on, prior to independence, from 1925-26; 
the Congress Party had been doing that earlier, at its Karachi Session, at its 
Madras Session. These were mainly discussing only the Fundamental Rights, 
as also the fact as to what exactly should be the socialistic policy of the 
States. Certain guarantee:; are given outright; certain guarantees are 
contemplated through State legislation. When we started framing the 
Constitution, after we became independent, the Constitution-makers were 
doubtful as to whether we had the capacity to make Part -IV also enforceable. 
They thought, if that was made enfor ceable, we would be creating a situation 
which will lead to an impasse. That is why Part -IV was not made enforceable. 
First, we have to consider article 41, wherein the right to work, to education 
and to public assistance in certain cases is provided. But it does not provide 
the right to employment. It provides only the right to work. It does not 
envisage a situation where every citizen'will have a certain position, where he 
would be able to get some employment. 
Government giving employment and a person finding employment for 
himself out of favourable situations visible in society are two different things. 
Government providing employment for everyone in society today -would be an 
impossible task. I would, therefore, suggest that Shri Pachouri should make a 
suitable amendment in his Bill that it would really not provide employment but it 
would provide the right to work. One of the clauses proposed in the Bill, that 
is, dause7, contemplates that in regard to service there would be a right to 
promotion because the Bill conceives that this will be Hke any other 
employment in government. There is a proposal in the Bill that there should be 
promotion. Clause 7 in the proposed Bill, for instance, contemplates, and I 
read: "It shall be obligatory on the part of the State to ensure periodical 
promotions to all employees on the basis of the test of their performance."  I 
don't think that this can be supported.   The support

auto-promotion should be available. It means you undertake work, perform 
better, earn more, feel free and live happily. There, a person with the right to 
work would get promotional advantages. Therefore, basically, there is no 
employment as contemplated that the employer would be providing 
employment, and the obligation that the society would be able to fulfil in terms 
of article 41 would be the right to work. Article 41 reads like this. "The State 
shall, within the limits of its economic capacity  and development, make 
effective provision for securing the right to work." Therefore, this is all that is 
contemplated in article 41. Based on the obligation of the State through 
legislation, through other manner of progress, economic development and an 
assessment of the situation, the State can provide the right to work. This right 
to work would, really, depend upon one's capacity to work, one's ability to 
perform - education being the mechanism or the machinery through which all 
these would be acquired by a citizen. I remember a direct instance which I 
would like to place before your:kind consideration. I knew a washerman; he 
was engaged by my father -in-law who was a judge. 1 also became a judge in 
due course. I was satisfied that he was doing the work very well. I sent for him 
and asked: "Why don't you work for me?" He agreed to it and joined me for 
washing my clothes. Ten years after, when I was the Chief Justice in Orissa, 
he came to me saying, "Sir, I want to go out of this arrangement as I will not 
be able to work for you any more." When I asked him why, he said, "I have 
five sons. On the basis of reservation, one of my sons got into a Government 
job. I made one son read up to Intermediate, but he left it half way. The other 
two are good-for -nothing boys. The last is still in school, but he is not getting 
promoted every year. The two sons, who passed their Intermediate are not 
agreeable to washing clothes. They are not even agreeable to delivering the 
clothes which were treated at home and to be taken t o the washing ghat, 
saying, 'Friends will see us on the road and laugh at us when we are doing 
this job.' " 
Education instead of making one more effective to get employment, 
instead of making one more definite to do some service, takes away one's 
capacity to serve. It leads you half way. I remember Bharthruhari once having 
said, "As regards those who are very well educated, it is very easy to explain 
to them. It is also easy to explain to those who are not educated, because 
they begin from nothing..."

Half-way, people are very difficult to be convinced because they 
think they know everything and yet they do not know. But their own 
assessment of themselves is very difficult to accept. These people who are 
getting educated half -way are becoming unfit foi any employment. On that

point to taken note of. In India there: are some uneducaUid people in the

rural areas the unemployment is less than two per cent. In the ur ban areas, it 
accounts for four per cent, leaving aside the argument with regard to

comes to the city, he may be prepared even to  sell bananas on  a

four-wheeler. In this way, he may be doing some business, a small business. 
But, on the other hand, educated people who are graduates or postgraduates 
may only look for white-collar jobs. The educational system, the curriculum in 
this which they have studied has not inculcated into them some sort of self -
confidence of taking risk. Therefore, what I feel is that our educational system 
should be changed and curriculum should be changed in suc h a way that 
when a student comes out of a school or a college, he does not depend on

Labour Organisation Convention Number 182 passed, unanimously, by 174 
countries. It is regarding child labour. It comes under social clause and the 
developed countries are now pushing it on our shoulder s. This Convention 
was passed and ratified by the Republic of Seychelles. They were able to 
pass it, but child labour still exists in other countries. Sir, when the adults are 
not able to get any employment, how can we expect that children will get any 
job? This clearly shows that if children are given employment, they can be 
paid less remuneration. Children are satisfied with the remuneration they get, 
and, moreover, they cannot fight with their employer. These types of things 
are going on throughout the w orld. According to the International Labour 
Organisation, about 250 million children are actually in economic activity. That 
means, the children are, unfortunately, forced to work in tender age. This is 
the side affect of the unemployment. Even though we have got employment 
exchanges and even though there are rules that compulsory notification has 
to be issued for vacancies, etc., we cannot get, from any employment 
exchange, the correct statistics. That is the problem. The other problem is, if a 
person joins some private establishment, he is not intimating his appointment 
to the employment exchange. There is a law. The law says that if any concern 
employs more than 25 persons, the Employment Exchange (Compulsory 
Notification of Vacancies) Act is applicable. But, in practice, it is not so. 
Therefore, the statistics that you are getting from the employment exchanges, 
I feel, are not reflecting the real situation of unemployment in this country.

interaction with the states from where they can get all these things.  Sir, even 
the minimum wages, because of this

the Government of Japan before the USA

this, 55 per cent is in the service sector. Even within the organised sector, 55

what I feel is that new employment opportunities have to be created. Mere 
development of the Information Technology sector will not solve the problem 
totally. I agree that it will solve the problem to some extent, but we will not be 
able to solve the problem totally, by merely developing this sector. Another 
thing is that the people have to be educated, particularly, the women folk. For 
the proper implementation of the family planning programme, I think the 
education of girls is a must. The success of the family planning programme is 
based on the actual implementatL. f the education plan. If the education 
programme of the Government is successful, that too with regard to girls, 
automatically, the family planning programme will be successful. Therefore, if 
we want to implement .the family planning programme successfully, we must 
see that the programme of women's education actually succeed to the level 
that we have t argeted. There is a gap between the growth of birth-rate and 
growth of employment opportunities. According to the National Sample Survey 
Organisation, it is 2.37%, less than 2.4%. However, in the 9th Five-Year -Plan, 
it is expected that it would be around 2.44%. Sir, when there is a gap between 
the growth of birth-rate and growth of employment opportunities, 1 think 
unemployment will automatically increase. If the employable population is 
more than the employment opportunities, the effect would be that a lar ge 
number of people would remain unemployed. Therefor, the growth of 
employment opportunities has to supersede the employable population. Sir, I 
would like to suggest that this unemployment problem can be tackled by 
developing education, developing the inf ormation technology and instilling 
confidence among the youths. And, Sir, the most important thing is that the 
risk-taking attitude should be inculcated in the educated people. If all these 
things can be taken together, I think 60-70% of the unemployment problem 
can be solved within a decade; not immediately. Therefore, the Government 
should concentrate on all these things. Apart from that, Sir, I feel the 
employment opportunities in the public sector are going down. It is less than 
1%. However, the employm ent opportunities in the private sector are going 
up. It is more than 2%. When employment opportunities in the public sector 
reduces, Sir, the sufferers are those people who have been oppressed for 
centuries together in the name of religion and caste. I feel, reservation is 
necessary for them. In order to see that these people are not deprived of 
employment, this reservation policy has actually ;en brought up.  Now, since 
the employment opportunities in the public sector are

people may not get enough chances of <anployment. Sir, when we are 
seeking ways and means for the redressal of this problem, I think all these

SHRI T.N. CHATURVEDI (Uttar  Pradesh): Thank you, Mr. Vice-
Chairman, Sir, for giving me this opportunity to speak. I rise to support the 
objectives and the spirit of the Eradication of Unemployment Bill, 1996 which 
has been moved by the hon. Member, Shri Suresh Pachouri. Sir, the iss ue of 
unemployment is very explosive, and this issue has been with us for a very 
long time. This was an issue which agitated the minds of the intelligentsia in 
this country before the attainment of independence. If we see the objectives of 
the First Five Y ear Plan, we will find that the control or eradication or 
containment of the problem of unemployment was one of the basic objectives. 
Somehow, it so happened that during the Second Plan, the problem 
became much more acute and, at that time, some serious thinking was given, 
taking into account the situation then prevailing. Since then, unfortunately, 
from plan to plan, this problem, somehow or the other, has assumed a 
proportion which ehides our grasp and eludes any effort at controlling it. This 
problem is a rural problem; it is a problem of agriculture; it is a problem of the 
urban areas and of the cities. Sir, the root of the problem lies in what has been 
called poverty. Poverty in the rural areas and poverty in the urban areas is a 
continuous process. There is no dichotomy in it. The poor people are in search 
of employment, and for better avenues, they migrate to the cities. It is a 
question of the slums and the accompanying problems that arise from it. So, 
Sir, the approach to this problem of unemployment  will have to be a very 
integrated and a very holistic one. It is directly intertwined with the question of 
the process of development, the nature of development, the direction of 
development and how the fruits of development reach every section of the 
society. We have just heard Smt. Jamana Devi Barupal lamenting about 
certain sections of the society, particularly, the Scheduled Tribes, being 
deprived of the benefits which ought to have flowed to them in the wake of 
freedom.    Sir, this

submitted to the Jute Manufacturing Development Council, Calcutta and also 
to the Ministry  of Textile, Government of India. This is a very, very important 
document. 
"Jute is a natural product; it is bio -degradable; and it causes very little 
environmental pollution. Poly sacks impose heavy burden on the environment. 
Jute sacks have a life cycle that begins with farming, a way of life and a 
means of livelihood for about four million Indians. Poly sacks, on the other 
hand, are derivative of oil, a non-renewable natural resource, the exploitation 
of which has an opportunity cost for the future gener ations. The number of 
reuses and effective life of a jute sack more than compensate its weight and 
first-cost disadvantages compared to a poly sack, when one considers the life 
cycle cost relative to the weight and value of materials handled during the lif e 
time. Jute, thus, helps sustainable development. Today, when the world is 
trying to evolve ways and means for sustainable development, India has 
natural advantage in its jute industry, that not only supports livelihood of 
millions of people, is environmental friendly, but is also cost -worthy." So, in 
this report that has been submitted by the Indian Institute of Technology, 
Kharagpur to the Jute Manufactures Development Council, Calcutta, they 
have made their observations and very good recommendations on how it can 
be utilised and what the Government
